newsitem.title: INDIA: India said needs 20 pct oil product price rise.
newsitem.headline: India said needs 20 pct oil product price rise.

text.p: India's new centre-left government will need to raise domestic prices of major petroleum products by an average 20 percent to curb its runaway subsidy bill, analysts and economists said on Sunday.
"The options are to basically to raise the prices of diesel and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) quite significantly and some increase in petrol," oil analyst Y.R. Mehta said.
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Thursday the government needed to take a bold decision to contain a high oil pool deficit arising from subsidised prices.
Gujral said he would need the nation's support in tackling the deficit, pegged at 155 billion rupees ($4.32 billion) at the end of 1996/97 (April-March).

India's oil pool account reconciles the state-fixed administered pricing mechanism with free market conditions. It acts as a balancing mechanism whereby refineries are compensated for subsidised prices.

"You cannot go on living with this kind of deficit that you are soon reaching a stage where you do not have the money to buy. I do not want to reach that stage," Gujral told state television in an interview.
Petroleum ministry officials said the government was unlikely to increase oil prices before parliament adjourned in mid-May.
"We can look forward to something after May 15," said one official.

"A 20 percent increase in diesel and LPG is a must," Mehta said, adding that the country's diesel consumption was much higher than that of petrol. "Revenue will come only if you increase diesel prices."
He said India consumed about 30 million tonnes of diesel and six million tonnes of petrol a year.

Petroleum Ministry officials said the total subsidy on petroleum products in 1996/97 (April-March) was estimated at 184 billion rupees, including 83 billion rupees on kerosene and 64 billion on diesel.
"I think they will have to increase the prices. There is no other choice," said Shashank Bhide, of the National Council of Applied Economic Research.
Bhide said prices would have to be raised 20-25 percent on petrol, diesel and LPG while it was difficult to say how far the government would go with kerosene.
Bhide said the government would either try to wipe out the deficit or reduce it to the bare minimum.
India raised petroleum product prices last July. The decision was criticised by the Congress and left-wing parties and sparked country-wide protests.
The main opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party on Friday said the government should convene a meeting of major political parties before deciding to raise prices.
Analysts said the state-run Indian Oil Corporation would exhaust its external commercial borrowing limit of $2.9 billion by June 30 and come under pressure on import pricing.
"I think the price rise will come within the next two months or so," Bhide said.
